 These countries affected by El Niño, from Peru to Kenya, show how one warm Pacific pattern can bring floods, drought, wildfires and crop losses across the tropics and beyond
 1 / 14 List slides From Peru to Kenya: 12 countries affected by El Niño List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 4, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 A band of unusually warm water in the Pacific Ocean can empty reservoirs in South America, feed fires in Southeast Asia and swell rivers in East Africa. That band has a name, El Niño, and it returns every few years.
 The name is Spanish for "the boy" or "the Christ child." Peruvian fishermen gave it to a warm current that appeared off their coast around Christmas. Scientists now use it for a broader event: a warming of sea-surface waters across the central and eastern tropical Pacific.
 El Niño recurs irregularly, roughly every two to seven years. A typical episode lasts about nine to 12 months. It is the warm phase of a larger climate cycle known as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO. Its cool counterpart is La Niña.
 The main way El Niño reaches distant countries is through rainfall. As the warm water shifts east, the zones of rising air and heavy storms shift with it. Some regions turn wetter than usual, with heavy rain and flooding. Others turn drier, with drought, low rivers and higher fire risk. The pattern is not fixed. Two El Niño events can play out differently, and a country that floods in one episode may escape the next.
 Those shifts carry economic consequences. Fisheries, farms, hydropower dams, shipping routes and city water systems all depend on rain arriving when expected. When it doesn't, the effects can travel through food prices, electricity supply and trade.
 Three strong events are widely cited as reference points: 1982–83, 1997–98 and 2015–16. Several of the countries below also felt the more recent 2023–24 El Niño.
 This list covers 12 countries affected by El Niño, grouped by region. It starts with Peru and Ecuador on South America's Pacific coast, then moves through the rest of the Americas, Southeast Asia, Oceania, South Asia and Africa. It is a selection, not a ranking, and not a complete list. Each entry describes what El Niño tends to bring to that country, along with documented episodes. Weather is rarely the only cause of a flood, a drought or a policy decision. Where El Niño played a part, it is treated as one factor among others.
 Peru: El Niño floods the north coast and disrupts the anchovy fishery 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Peru tends to take two hits in a strong El Niño year. Warm water disrupts the anchovy fishery behind its fishmeal industry, and heavy rain floods a northern coast that is usually desert.
 Both effects trace back to the ocean off Peru's shore. In normal years, the Humboldt Current and coastal upwelling bring cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface. That water supports plankton, which feeds vast schools of Peruvian anchovy, known locally as anchoveta. The species, Engraulis ringens, supports a single-species fishery that ranks among the world's biggest by catch volume.
 When El Niño warms the coastal sea, upwelling weakens and the cold water retreats. Anchovy schools tend to move deeper or farther south in search of cooler conditions. Catches can fall sharply as a result. Seabirds that feed on the anchovy, such as the Peruvian booby and the Guanay cormorant, also go hungry.
 The effects reach well beyond Peru. Most of the anchovy catch is processed into fishmeal and fish oil rather than eaten directly. Peru is one of the world's largest producers of fishmeal, which goes into feed for farmed fish, pigs and poultry. A poor season off Peru can tighten feed supplies for fish farms on other continents.
 The fishery has a long history with El Niño. The 1972–73 event, combined with heavy fishing pressure, contributed to a collapse of the anchovy stock. Today, Peruvian authorities set fishing seasons and catch limits based on scientific surveys of the stock. In warm years, those surveys can lead to delayed or shortened seasons.
 On land, the problem is too much water. Northern regions such as Piura and Tumbes normally receive little rain. Much of Piura sits on the Sechura Desert. During strong El Niño events, warm offshore water fuels downpours that swell dry riverbeds and overwhelm towns built for arid conditions.
 The 1997–98 El Niño brought severe rains to northern Peru. Flooding damaged roads, bridges, homes and farmland across the region.
 In 2017, a different kind of event struck. It was classified as a coastal El Niño, or Niño Costero. The warming was concentrated near the coasts of Peru and Ecuador rather than across the wider Pacific. It still caused serious flooding across northern Peru. Mudslides, known in Peru as huaicos, swept through communities in the region.
 Peru also runs a national monitoring system for these coastal conditions. It issues alerts when warming develops offshore, giving fishing fleets and northern towns advance notice.
 Ecuador: coastal flooding and warm-water stress in the Galápagos 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Ecuador feels El Niño in two places at once. Strong events tend to bring heavy rain and flooding to its Pacific coast, while warmer seas around the Galápagos Islands cut off the cold-water food supply that much of the islands' wildlife depends on.
 The mainland coast is where people bear most of the impact. Provinces such as Esmeraldas, Manabí, Guayas and El Oro sit on a low coastal plain that drains toward the Pacific. In normal years, much of the southern stretch of that coast is relatively dry. During a strong El Niño, warm water offshore feeds intense, repeated downpours. Rivers and drainage systems cannot carry that much water away.
 The 1997–98 event remains the reference point for coastal flooding in Ecuador. Months of heavy rain flooded towns, triggered landslides and washed out roads and bridges along the coast. Broken transport links cut off communities. They also slowed the movement of goods to and from Guayaquil, the country's largest city and main port.
 Agriculture on the coast is exposed as well. The lowlands grow much of the country's export produce, including bananas. Ecuador ranks among the world's largest banana exporters. Flooded plantations and waterlogged soils reduce harvests in a wet El Niño year. Damaged roads make it harder to move whatever fruit survives to the docks.
 About 900 kilometers offshore, the Galápagos face a different problem. The islands' marine life relies on cold, nutrient-rich water. The Humboldt Current carries some of it north. The Equatorial Undercurrent pushes more of it up from the depths along the western islands. When El Niño warms the surface, that upwelling weakens, and the food chain thins out from the bottom up.
 Marine iguanas show the effect clearly. They are the only lizards in the world that forage in the sea, grazing on algae along rocky shorelines. In warm-water years, the red and green algae they prefer die back, and many iguanas starve. Their numbers fell sharply during the strong events of 1982–83 and 1997–98.
 Galápagos sea lions struggle too. The fish they hunt move deeper or scatter. Mothers must then travel farther to feed. Pups and juveniles are the most vulnerable, and many die when food runs short. Galápagos penguins and flightless cormorants also depend on cold-water prey. Both suffered heavy losses in 1982–83.
 Not every species loses out. Heavy rain turns the normally arid islands green, and land plants, insects and seed-eating finches can multiply. That split between hardship at sea and abundance on land has made the Galápagos a long-running field site for studying how El Niño reshapes an ecosystem.
 Colombia: El Niño drought, low reservoirs and Bogotá water rationing 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Colombia tends to turn drier during El Niño. That matters for a country that gets most of its electricity from hydropower. Weak rainfall drains the reservoirs that supply both power stations and city taps. In April 2024, low reservoirs pushed Bogotá into water rationing.
 The country's geography explains the exposure. The Andes split into three ranges across Colombia, and rivers descending from them feed a network of hydroelectric dams. Much of the Andean region also has two rainy seasons each year. Those wet spells refill the reservoirs before the drier months.
 When El Niño weakens that rainfall, storage falls. The electricity grid then leans harder on thermal plants that burn gas and coal. Those plants cost more to run. Dry years tend to push up wholesale power prices.
 Colombia has seen how far that pressure can go. A drought linked to El Niño left reservoirs low in 1992, and the government imposed nationwide electricity rationing. Scheduled blackouts ran for months. Clocks were moved forward an hour to save power, a change known as "la hora Gaviria" after then-President César Gaviria.
 Bogotá's 2024 shortage hit water supply rather than power. Most of the capital's drinking water comes from the Chingaza system, a set of reservoirs and tunnels in the mountains east of the city. Months of weak rainfall left its storage at low levels.
 The city divided its service area into sectors. Each sector took turns going without water for a day at a time. Residents were also asked to cut their consumption.
 The dry spell overlapped with the 2023–24 El Niño, which contributed to the shortfall. It was not the sole cause. Bogotá is one of South America's largest cities. With one main system supplying most of its water, low storage at Chingaza affected millions of residents.
 Water stress reaches farms as well. Colombia is one of the world's leading coffee producers. Its growers depend on the timing of rain for flowering and bean development. A prolonged dry season can disrupt that cycle and reduce yields.
 For Colombia, much of El Niño's impact comes down to storage. Whether the country gets through an event without cuts depends heavily on how full its reservoirs are when the dry conditions arrive.
 Brazil: Amazon drought in the north and heavier rain in the south 
 Illustration: Quartz
 El Niño tends to split Brazil in two. Much of the north, including the Amazon $AMZN basin, usually turns drier than normal, while the south tends to get more rain.
 That divide matters in a country of Brazil's size. A single event can leave river towns in the Amazon short of water. The same event can push farm states in the far south toward waterlogged fields.
 The Rio Negro offers a recent example of the northern side. In October 2023, during an El Niño year, the river at Manaus fell to its lowest level on record. Manaus is the capital of Amazonas state and the largest city in the Brazilian Amazon .
 The Rio Negro joins the Solimões River near Manaus, and together they form the main stem of the Amazon . Across much of the region, rivers do the work of roads. Boats carry fuel, food, medicine and passengers between communities that have no highway links. When water levels drop, some channels become too shallow for those boats. Riverside settlements can then be cut off from supplies.
 The Rio Negro drains a vast catchment, and its level reflects rainfall across that whole area. El Niño was underway in 2023, but it was not the only factor shaping that year's dry season.
 Drier conditions in the Amazon also raise fire risk. Most fires in the region are set by people, often to clear land for pasture or crops. A parched forest allows those fires to spread farther than they would in a wet year.
 The semi-arid interior of northeastern Brazil, known as the sertão, also tends toward drought in El Niño years. Smallholder farmers and livestock herders there depend on short seasonal rains. A weak rainy season can cut harvests and strain local water supplies.
 The pattern reverses in the south. States such as Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina and Paraná tend to see above-average rainfall during El Niño. These states are major producers of soybeans, corn and rice. Rio Grande do Sul grows the largest share of Brazil's rice.
 Extra rain can delay planting and harvests. It also raises the risk of river flooding in low-lying towns and farmland.
 Southern Brazil has flooded in El Niño years, but each flood has several drivers. Local storms, terrain, drainage and land use all play a part. El Niño shifts the odds toward a wetter south. It does not decide the outcome of any single storm.
 Effects in Brazil's center and southeast vary more from one event to the next. The north–south contrast is the most consistent El Niño signal in the country.
 Panama: how El Niño drought contributed to Panama Canal transit cuts 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A severe drought in 2023, to which El Niño contributed, led the Panama Canal Authority to cut daily ship crossings and lower draft limits. Shallower drafts meant many vessels had to carry less cargo to make the passage.
 The canal's exposure to drought comes from its design. Since it opened in 1914, the waterway has relied on locks that lift ships up to Gatún Lake and lower them again. Gatún Lake is an artificial reservoir created by damming the Chagres River. When it was completed, it was the largest man-made lake in the world.
 Every transit draws on that lake. Gravity moves fresh water from the lake into the lock chambers. That water then flows out to the ocean. The original locks use no pumps to send it back. A long run of ships therefore means a steady drain on the reservoir.
 The same lake system also supplies drinking water to much of Panama's population, including Panama City. In a dry year, the canal's needs compete directly with household supply.
 Panama depends on its rainy season, which usually runs from about May to December, to refill the reservoir. El Niño tends to bring drier conditions to parts of Central America. In 2023, rainfall fell well short, and the lake dropped low enough that the authority rationed passage.
 The newer, larger locks opened in 2016 after an expansion project. They include water-saving basins that reuse part of the water from each lockage. Ships using the older locks have no such system.
 The restrictions rippled through global shipping. Vessels waited at anchor for slots, and some operators paid extra in auctions for priority crossings. Others sent ships on longer routes, including through the Suez Canal or around the southern tip of South America.
 The canal links the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. It is a key route for cargo moving between the U.S. East and Gulf coasts and Asia. That reach helps explain why a rainfall shortfall in one Central American country registered in freight markets worldwide.
 Indonesia: peatland fires, haze and rice losses in El Niño years 
 Illustration: Quartz
 In Indonesia, El Niño tends to bring a longer, harsher dry season. That raises the risk of fire on the country's carbon-rich peatlands. The 2015 El Niño coincided with major fires that sent thick haze across much of Southeast Asia.
 Peat is a waterlogged soil built from layers of partly decayed plant matter. Indonesia holds one of the largest areas of tropical peatland in the world. Most of it lies on Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua. In its natural state, peat stays wet and resists burning.
 Much of that land has been drained with canals to grow oil palm and pulpwood trees. Drained peat dries out, and in a drought year it ignites easily. Land is often cleared by burning, and those fires can spread into the dry peat nearby.
 Peat fires are hard to put out. They can smolder underground for weeks, out of reach of water dropped from aircraft. They also release large amounts of carbon dioxide and dense smoke.
 That smoke crosses borders. In 2015, haze from Indonesian fires drifted over Singapore, Malaysia and other neighbors, disrupting flights and daily life. The strong 1997–98 El Niño had produced a similar regional haze crisis.
 Earlier haze episodes led governments to respond with laws and agreements. Singapore passed its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act in 2014. The law allows penalties against companies that cause haze affecting the city-state. Indonesia's parliament ratified the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution later that year. In early 2016, President Joko Widodo created a Peatland Restoration Agency to rewet and restore damaged peat.
 Farms feel the dry spells as well. Rice is Indonesia's staple food, and much of the crop depends on the timing of the rainy season. When the rains arrive late or fall short, planting is delayed and harvests can shrink.
 A weaker harvest puts pressure on the national food supply. Bulog, the state logistics agency, manages rice stocks and imports. Those reserves act as a buffer when domestic output falls. In El Niño years, the same dry weather that feeds the fires can also tighten the country's rice supply.
 Philippines: dry spells and farm losses during the 2015–16 El Niño 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 2015–16 El Niño left farms across the Philippines short of rain, and prolonged dry spells damaged crops in several regions. Farming in the country depends heavily on seasonal rainfall. A dry El Niño year can mean smaller harvests and lower rural incomes.
 The Philippines is an archipelago of more than 7,000 islands in the western Pacific. Much of its rain arrives with the southwest monsoon, known locally as habagat, and with tropical storms. In El Niño years, rainfall across much of the country tends to drop below normal. The effect is not uniform, and some provinces fare worse than others from one event to the next.
 The drying effect of the 2015–16 event stretched into the early months of 2016. That period overlapped with the country's usual dry season, when fields already receive little rain.
 Rice is the national staple, and most of it comes from small family farms. Many paddies depend on rainfall rather than irrigation canals. When the rains fail, farmers may delay planting, and crops already in the ground can wither before harvest.
 Corn is the country's second major grain crop, and Mindanao, the large southern island group, grows a substantial share of it. Much of that corn is rainfed. Parts of Mindanao were among the farming areas hit by drought during the 2015–16 event.
 Irrigated land is not fully shielded either. Angat Dam in Bulacan province supplies most of Metro Manila's water. It also feeds irrigation for farmland in Bulacan and Pampanga. When its reservoir runs low, cities and farms compete for the same supply.
 For a farming household, a failed crop cuts into both its food supply and its cash income in the same season. Smallholders with little savings have limited room to absorb that loss before the next planting.
 Domestic rice production does not fully meet demand, and the Philippines imports rice to cover the gap. Any shortfall in local harvests has to be made up from domestic stocks or imports.
 Papua New Guinea: drought and frost in the highlands in 2015–16 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 2015–16 El Niño brought drought and frost to Papua New Guinea's highlands. Both damaged the food gardens that most families there rely on. The combination hit communities that grow nearly everything they eat and keep little stored surplus.
 The highlands form a chain of mountain valleys running through the center of the island of New Guinea. Provinces such as Enga, Hela, Southern Highlands, Western Highlands, Simbu and Eastern Highlands hold a large share of the country's population. Many of these valleys sit far above the coastal lowlands. That altitude gives them a cooler climate than the rest of the tropical country. Most people there live in rural villages rather than towns.
 Sweet potato, known locally as kaukau, is the staple crop across much of the region. Families plant it in mounded gardens and harvest it continuously rather than in a single season. That system works when rain is reliable. It leaves households exposed when gardens stop producing for months at a time.
 Frost is the less expected threat in a tropical country. Dry spells tend to bring clear night skies, and clear skies let heat escape from the ground after dark. In high-altitude valleys, temperatures can then drop below freezing. Frost burns sweet potato leaves and can kill the plants outright. The resulting losses show up in harvests well after the cold nights have ended.
 Drought added a second strain. Streams and springs that supply drinking water ran low in many areas. Gardens planted in dry soil struggled to establish.
 The pattern was not new. The 1997–98 El Niño brought a similar run of drought and frost to the highlands. In that event, crop failures led to widespread food shortages across the region.
 The effects of the 2015 dry spell also reached beyond village gardens. Low water on the Fly River in Western Province halted barge traffic that year. The Ok Tedi copper and gold mine suspended operations because it could not ship its concentrate downriver. The mine is one of Papua New Guinea's largest export earners.
 Australia: drier winters, bushfire risk and Great Barrier Reef bleaching 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Eastern and northern Australia tend to receive less rain in winter and spring during El Niño years. That dry tilt raises bushfire danger and strains farms. It has also coincided with mass coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef.
 The timing matters for agriculture. Wheat and barley in the eastern grain belt are sown in autumn. These crops depend on winter and spring rain to fill out before harvest. A dry season at that stage can cut yields sharply. Livestock producers face a parallel problem as pasture dries out, and some sell animals they can no longer feed.
 Fire risk climbs alongside the dryness. Low rainfall leaves grass, scrub and forest litter parched heading into the warmer months. El Niño years also tend to bring hotter days across southern Australia. That heat dries the fuel further. The result is a longer window in which a single ignition can spread quickly.
 El Niño is not the only driver of a bad fire season. The Indian Ocean Dipole, a separate pattern of sea-surface temperature differences across the Indian Ocean, also shapes Australian rainfall. A positive dipole tends to dry the southeast. The 2019–20 Black Summer fires burned during a strong positive dipole rather than an El Niño. When both patterns line up, the drying can compound.
 At sea, the effects show up on the Great Barrier Reef, the coral system stretching along the Queensland coast. Mass bleaching hit the reef in 1998 and again in 2016. Both episodes came at the tail end of strong El Niño events. Bleaching happens when water stays too warm for too long and corals expel the algae living in their tissue. Without those algae, corals lose their color and their main food source.
 Bleached coral can recover if temperatures fall soon enough. If the heat lasts, many corals die. The 2016 episode hit the reef's northern section hardest.
 Long-term ocean warming adds to the pressure. Each El Niño now arrives on top of higher baseline sea temperatures. The reef bleached again in 2017, a year without El Niño conditions. That repeat showed heat stress can bleach the reef without El Niño.
 India: a weaker monsoon and the 2023 rice export ban 
 Illustration: Quartz
 El Niño years tend to bring India a weaker southwest monsoon, the June-to-September rains that water most of the country's crops. A poor monsoon can shrink harvests and push up food prices across the world's most populous country.
 The southwest monsoon delivers the bulk of India's annual rainfall. Farmers time the kharif, or summer, planting season around its arrival. Rice, pulses, soybeans and cotton are among the crops sown as the rains begin. Much of India's cropland has no irrigation and relies on rainfall alone. A late or patchy monsoon therefore reaches farm incomes quickly.
 The link is a tendency, not a rule. Several of India's notable drought years, including 2002 and 2009, coincided with El Niño. The strong 1997–98 event, by contrast, passed with a roughly normal monsoon. Conditions in the Indian Ocean matter too. A pattern called the Indian Ocean Dipole can offset or reinforce the Pacific signal. A positive phase of the dipole helped support the rains in 1997.
 That uncertainty shapes economic planning. India's weather agency issues a monsoon forecast each spring, and farmers and traders watch it closely. Food makes up a large share of the country's consumer price basket. A weak monsoon can feed directly into inflation.
 Rice sits at the center of these concerns. India is the world's largest rice exporter. At home, a public distribution system supplies subsidized grain to hundreds of millions of people. Any threat to the harvest touches both domestic food security and global trade.
 In July 2023, India's government banned exports of non-basmati white rice. The move came amid concerns about domestic supply and rising prices. It arrived as an El Niño was developing in the Pacific. NOAA had declared El Niño conditions in June 2023. Basmati rice was not covered by the ban.
 The decision's effects reached well beyond India. Many importing countries in Asia and Africa depend on Indian rice. Buyers turned to other exporters such as Thailand and Vietnam. International rice prices climbed in the months that followed.
 A weak monsoon also affects water beyond the farm. Lower rainfall reduces reservoir storage and slows the recharge of groundwater. That puts pressure on drinking water supplies and on hydropower output in the dry months before the next monsoon.
 Zambia: 2023–24 drought, a national disaster and Kariba hydropower cuts 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Zambia felt the 2023–24 El Niño through a severe drought that spread across southern Africa. The government declared the drought a national disaster in early 2024, and low water in the Zambezi basin cut hydropower generation at Kariba.
 Southern Africa's main rainy season runs roughly from November to April. El Niño tends to suppress rainfall across the region during those months. In Zambia, the dry spell struck during the growing season, when crops depended most on rain.
 President Hakainde Hichilema made the disaster declaration. The step allows a government to redirect public funds and appeal for outside assistance. Neighboring Zimbabwe and Malawi also declared disasters as the drought deepened across the region.
 Maize is Zambia's staple crop. It is the base of nshima, the stiff porridge served at most meals. Most Zambian farmers work small plots and rely on rainfall rather than irrigation. That leaves harvests exposed when the rains fail. The drought damaged crops in many farming areas.
 The second blow fell on electricity. Zambia generates the large majority of its power from hydroelectric plants. The biggest of these draws on Lake Kariba, the reservoir behind Kariba Dam on the Zambezi River.
 Kariba Dam was completed in the late 1950s and straddles the border with Zimbabwe. The two countries manage the reservoir jointly through the Zambezi River Authority. Power stations on each bank draw from the same body of water.
 Weak inflows during the drought left less water available for generation. The Zambezi River Authority restricted how much water the power stations could use. ZESCO, Zambia's state-owned utility, responded with prolonged load-shedding. Households and businesses went without power for many hours a day.
 The shortages reached beyond homes. Copper is Zambia's main export, and its mines are among the country's largest electricity users. Small businesses that depend on grid power, from welders to barbers, also lost working hours.
 Zambia relies on rainfall for both its staple food and most of its electricity. During the 2023–24 drought, that dependence meant one poor rainy season strained the food supply and the power grid at the same time.
 Kenya: heavier short rains and floods in El Niño years 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Kenya tends to receive heavier-than-normal short rains during El Niño years. That rainy season runs from October to December. In strong events it has brought widespread flooding, including in 1997–98 and again in late 2023.
 Kenya has two main rainy seasons. The long rains fall roughly from March to May. The short rains arrive later in the year. El Niño's clearest signal in East Africa shows up in the second of these.
 Farmers and herders plan around both seasons. A shift in the short rains has direct consequences for planting and grazing.
 The 1997–98 episode showed how severe the impact can be. Rains far above normal fell across much of East Africa in late 1997. Rivers burst their banks, and roads and bridges washed out.
 The standing floodwater also created breeding grounds for mosquitoes. An outbreak of Rift Valley fever followed in northeastern Kenya and southern Somalia. The disease affects both livestock and people.
 Late 2023 repeated parts of that pattern. Heavy rains struck Kenya, Somalia and Ethiopia during the short-rains season. Northeastern Kenya, including counties along the Tana River, saw extensive flooding. Many families were displaced from their homes.
 The Indian Ocean plays a role too. A positive Indian Ocean Dipole — warmer water in the western Indian Ocean relative to the east — also tends to boost East African short rains. Both conditions were in place in late 2023. That overlap makes it inaccurate to credit El Niño alone for those floods.
 The 2023 rains also arrived at a difficult moment. They followed a drought that spanned five consecutive failed rainy seasons across the Horn of Africa. Dry, hardened soil absorbs water poorly. Heavy rain on that ground tends to run off rather than soak in. Pastoralists who had already lost livestock to drought then faced floods.
 La Niña tends to push the short rains the other way. The consecutive La Niña years from 2020 to 2023 were associated with that drought. For Kenya, the full ENSO cycle can mean swinging between too little rain and too much within a few years.
